rated-voltage: The rated voltage of a circuit-breaker is the highest r.m.s. phase-to-phase voltage at which it is designed to operate, defining the upper limit of service voltage. For HV AC circuit-breakers, sub-clause 4.1 of IEC Publication 694 applies directly ([[iec-56]] 4.1). Standard rated voltages follow internationally agreed series (Series I, based on general practice, and Series II, based on North-American 60 Hz practice). For example, the rated voltage 27 kV is also used in the United States and Canada. The rated voltage is the reference quantity that determines the power-frequency recovery voltage in breaking duties and fixes the [[rated-insulation-level]] (4.2), the standard values of [[transient-recovery-voltage]] (4.102), and the conditions defining the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] (4.101).
rated-insulation-level: The rated insulation level specifies the dielectric withstand capability of the circuit-breaker, expressed by rated power-frequency and impulse withstand voltages to earth, between poles, and across the open break. Sub-clause 4.2 of IEC Publication 694 applies, supplemented in [[iec-56]] 4.2. For [[rated-voltage]] up to and including 72.5 kV, Table I applies; Series II (60 Hz, USA/Canada) is added, e.g. 72.5 kV gives 350 kV rated lightning impulse withstand (peak) and 160 kV power-frequency withstand to earth (4.2.1). For 100-245 kV, Table III applies (4.2.2); for 300 kV and above, switching-impulse withstand voltages from Table IV apply (4.2.3), with an increased open-breaker value (column 6) for special circuit-breakers used in synchronizing with substantial switching surges. Coordinated with [[rated-voltage]].
rated-frequency: The rated frequency is the power-system frequency for which the circuit-breaker is designed and at which all rated quantities apply. Sub-clause 4.3 of IEC Publication 694 is applicable ([[iec-56]] 4.3). The standard rated frequencies are 50 Hz and 60 Hz. Rated frequency is load-bearing for several other ratings: the d.c. component of the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] is referenced to a half-cycle of rated frequency for auxiliary-power tripping (4.101.2); the [[rated-short-circuit-making-current]] multiplier is 2.5x at 50 Hz versus 2.6x at 60 Hz (4.103); and the standard [[transient-recovery-voltage]] values apply to service frequencies of 50 Hz or 60 Hz (4.102). The standard [[rated-operating-sequence]] time intervals are likewise tied to rated frequency.
rated-normal-current:
The rated normal current is the r.m.s. value of current the circuit-breaker can carry continuously at rated frequency without its temperature rise exceeding the limits of Table V of IEC Publication 694. Sub-clauses 4.4.1 and 4.4.2 of IEC 694 apply, with additions in [[iec-56]] 4.4. Values shall be selected from the standard R 10 series:
- 400 A; 630 A; 800 A; 1250 A; 1600 A; 2000 A; 2500 A; 3150 A; 4000 A; 5000 A; 6300 A.
Higher values, if required, are also taken from the R 10 series. Where a series-connected accessory such as a direct over-current release is fitted, its rated normal current is the r.m.s. current it carries continuously without deterioration. Carrying capability is verified against the [[rated-short-time-withstand-current]] (4.5) and temperature-rise limits.
rated-short-time-withstand-current: The rated short-time withstand current is the r.m.s. value of current the circuit-breaker can carry, in the closed position, for the [[rated-duration-of-short-circuit]] without damage, under prescribed conditions. Sub-clause 4.5 of IEC Publication 694 applies with the addition that the rated short-time withstand current is equal to the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] ([[iec-56]] 4.5, see 4.101). It therefore takes its standard values from the same R 10 series of a.c. components (6.3, 8, 10, 12.5, 16, 20, 25, 31.5, 40, 50, 63, 80, 100 kA). The thermal stress it represents is associated with the [[rated-peak-withstand-current]] (4.6), which expresses the corresponding electrodynamic (peak) stress. Verified by short-time withstand current tests (6.5).
rated-peak-withstand-current: The rated peak withstand current is the peak value of the first major loop of current the circuit-breaker can withstand in the closed position during a short-circuit, representing the electrodynamic (mechanical) stress. Sub-clause 4.6 of IEC Publication 694 applies, with the addition that the rated peak withstand current is equal to the [[rated-short-circuit-making-current]] ([[iec-56]] 4.6, see 4.103). It is therefore derived as 2.5x (50 Hz) or 2.6x (60 Hz) the r.m.s. a.c. component of the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]]. It complements the [[rated-short-time-withstand-current]] (4.5), which expresses the thermal stress carried for the [[rated-duration-of-short-circuit]] (4.7). Both are demonstrated together in the short-time and peak withstand current tests (6.5).
rated-duration-of-short-circuit: The rated duration of short-circuit is the time interval for which the circuit-breaker can carry, in the closed position, a current equal to its [[rated-short-time-withstand-current]] (4.5). Sub-clause 4.7 of IEC Publication 694 applies, with an addition in [[iec-56]] 4.7. A rated duration need not be assigned to a circuit-breaker fitted with a direct over-current release, provided that, in a circuit whose prospective breaking current equals its [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]], the circuit-breaker can carry the resulting current for the break-time required, with the over-current release set for its maximum time lag, while operating in accordance with its [[rated-operating-sequence]] (4.104). It thus links the thermal withstand rating to actual tripping behaviour and defines the duration associated with the [[rated-peak-withstand-current]].
rated-short-circuit-breaking-current:
The rated short-circuit breaking current is the highest short-circuit current the circuit-breaker can break under prescribed conditions, in a circuit whose power-frequency recovery voltage corresponds to its [[rated-voltage]] and whose [[transient-recovery-voltage]] equals the rated value of 4.102. For three-pole circuit-breakers the a.c. component relates to a three-phase short-circuit ([[iec-56]] 4.101). It is characterised by two values: the r.m.s. value of its a.c. component (the rated short-circuit current) and the percentage d.c. component (which may be ignored if it does not exceed 20%). The a.c. component is selected from the R 10 series:
- 6.3, 8, 10, 12.5, 16, 20, 25, 31.5, 40, 50, 63, 80, 100 kA (4.101.1).
The d.c. component corresponds to time interval t = minimum opening time (plus a half-cycle for auxiliary-power tripping), per Figure 9 (45 ms time constant). It equals the [[rated-short-time-withstand-current]] (4.5).
transient-recovery-voltage:
The rated transient recovery voltage (TRV) for terminal faults is the reference voltage that constitutes the limit of the prospective TRV of circuits the circuit-breaker can break on a fault at its terminals, relating to the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] (4.101). It is represented by a two-parameter envelope (uc, t3) for [[rated-voltage]] below 100 kV, or a four-parameter envelope (u1, t1, uc, t2) for 100 kV and above, plus a delay line (td) and, for the busbar-driven initial TRV (ITRV), a further line ([[iec-56]] 4.102). Standard values (prospective, for 50/60 Hz systems) include, from Table IIA (first-pole-to-clear factor 1.5):
- 12 kV: uc = 20.6 kV, t3 = 60 us, RRRV 0.34 kV/us
- 72.5 kV: uc = 124 kV, t3 = 166 us, RRRV 0.75 kV/us
For 100-170 kV (Table IIC, factor 1.3) e.g. 145 kV gives u1 = 154 kV, uc = 215 kV, RRRV 2.0 kV/us. ITRV may be neglected below 25 kA. Also governs [[short-line-fault]] supply-side TRV.
rated-short-circuit-making-current: The rated short-circuit making current is the peak current the circuit-breaker can close onto at its [[rated-voltage]] without damage, accounting for asymmetry at the instant of closing (see Figure 8). It shall be 2.5 times the r.m.s. value of the a.c. component of the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] for 50 Hz, and 2.6 times for 60 Hz ([[iec-56]] 4.103). The factor reflects the maximum asymmetrical peak arising from the d.c. offset at a 45 ms time constant and the chosen [[rated-frequency]]. The rated short-circuit making current is equal to the [[rated-peak-withstand-current]] (4.6), i.e. the closed-position electrodynamic withstand. It is demonstrated in short-circuit making and breaking tests performed according to the [[rated-operating-sequence]] (4.104).
rated-operating-sequence:
The rated operating sequence prescribes the standard succession of opening (O) and close-open (CO) operations the circuit-breaker must perform with specified time intervals. Two alternative sequences are defined ([[iec-56]] 4.104):
- a) O - t - CO - t' - CO, where t = 3 min for circuit-breakers not intended for rapid auto-reclosing, or t = 0.3 s (dead time) for those intended for rapid auto-reclosing, with t' = 3 min;
- b) CO - t'' - CO, with t'' = 15 s for circuit-breakers not intended for rapid auto-reclosing.
CO is a closing operation immediately followed by opening, with no intentional delay. For rapid auto-reclosing, alternative t' = 15 s (for [[rated-voltage]] up to 52 kV) and t' = 1 min are also used. If the dead time is adjustable, its limits shall be specified. This sequence governs short-circuit making and breaking test duties and applies to the [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] (4.101) and [[rated-duration-of-short-circuit]] (4.7).
short-line-fault: Rated characteristics for short-line faults are required for three-pole circuit-breakers designed for direct connection to overhead transmission lines, with [[rated-voltage]] of 52 kV and above and a [[rated-short-circuit-breaking-current]] exceeding 12.5 kA. They relate to breaking a single-phase earth fault in an earthed-neutral system ([[iec-56]] 4.105). The circuit comprises a source-side supply circuit and a load-side short line (Figure 13). The supply circuit has voltage U/sqrt(3), terminal-fault current equal to the rated short-circuit breaking current, prospective [[transient-recovery-voltage]] per Tables IVA/IVB/IVC, and ITRV from Table III. The line side is defined by standard rated surge impedance Z, peak factor k and time delay td (Table V), with the RRRV factor s = 0.200 kV/(us-kA) at 50 Hz and 0.240 at 60 Hz. TRV is calculated per Appendix AA; the initial portion is closely related to the ITRV described under 4.102.
